new.title: Read two centuries of style on Ghent's City Hall
new.desc: Ghent's town hall wears two faces. The lacy late Gothic wing was built between 1519 and 1539 to designs by Rombout II Keldermans, while the sober Renaissance facade on the Botermarkt went up between 1595 and 1618. The Pacification of Ghent was proclaimed in one of its halls in 1576.
new.tip: Stand on the corner of Hoogpoort and Botermarkt to see both styles meet. The Pacification Hall and other rooms are mostly seen on guided tours, so ask at the tourist office.

new.title: Step into Sint-Niklaaskerk, the first of the three towers
new.desc: Built from the 13th century in blue-grey Tournai stone, this church on the Korenmarkt is a textbook example of Scheldt Gothic. Its 76-metre lantern tower over the crossing pours light into the transept, and it is the first of the three towers you see lined up from Sint-Michielsbrug.
new.tip: The entrance is on Cataloniëstraat and visiting is free. Come on a quiet weekday morning, when the light falls down through the lantern tower and you have the nave almost to yourself.

new.title: Pass under Neptune at the Old Fish Market
new.desc: Opposite the Gravensteen, a baroque gateway crowned by Neptune leads into the market where Ghent's fishmongers traded until the 1960s; the figures beside him stand for the Scheldt and the Leie. Just inside, a glass floor shows remains of the medieval Sint-Veerle church, including a 1567 gravestone carved with 'COGITA MORI', remember death.
new.tip: The city's tourist office is inside, so this is the place to pick up maps or a CityCard Gent. Look down for the gravestone right after the gate.

new.title: Find the Devil's castle, Geeraard de Duivelsteen
new.desc: This stone residence from around 1225 is named after the knight Geeraard van Gent, nicknamed 'the Devil'. Over the centuries it served as an arsenal, a monastery, a school, an asylum, a prison and the state archive, and when it was turned into offices in 2025 builders found human remains under the floor of its old church.
new.tip: It is private offices now, so this is a walk around the outside. Fans of the Nero comics will recognise it as the Devil's home from several albums.

new.title: Have a coffee with cream at Mokabon
new.desc: Italian immigrant Erminio Mazzaro started roasting coffee here in 1937, and Mokabon calls itself Ghent's first coffee bar. The blends are still roasted every week to his recipe, and the coffee comes topped with fresh whipped cream.
new.tip: It is tiny, so expect to share a table with strangers. Buy a bag of freshly roasted beans on the way out.

new.title: Work through the beer list at Het Waterhuis aan de Bierkant
new.desc: On the corner of the Groentenmarkt, with the Leie flowing right past the windows, this café keeps a list of hundreds of Belgian beers. It is the classic place to taste your way from local brews to Trappists in one sitting.
new.tip: It is popular with visitors, so go in the early afternoon for a seat by the water, and ask the staff for a beer from a brewery you have never heard of.
new.q: Waterhuis aan de Bierkant Groentenmarkt 9 Gent

new.title: Buy bread at Himschoot, baking on the Groentenmarkt since 1880
new.desc: The ovens of Bakkerij Himschoot have been burning at Groentenmarkt 1 since 1880, which makes it probably the oldest bakery in Ghent. Locals queue under the old shopfront for bread, pastries and cakes.
new.tip: Go early at the weekend for the full choice. If you are exploring the docks, the newer Himschoot branch at Dok Noord bakes the same recipes.

new.title: Catch a late gig around the Vlasmarkt
new.desc: The Vlasmarkt is the centre of Ghent's night life all year round. Charlatan, a big alternative dance pub, books different acts every week, Kinky Star is a cornerstone of the local music scene, and more bars and clubs fill the rest of the square.
new.tip: Things only get going late in the evening. The morning after, the flea market on Sint-Jacobs is a few steps away from Friday to Sunday.

new.title: See what's new at Kunsthal Gent in the Caermersklooster
new.desc: Behind the walls of the 13th-century Caermersklooster, the old Carmelite monastery of the Patershol, Kunsthal Gent is a platform for contemporary art. On weekdays it is a workspace for artists; at weekends it opens as an exhibition venue.
new.tip: Entry is pay what you can. Go at the weekend, as other days are by appointment only, and look at how the exhibitions use the old monastery rooms.

new.title: Count the crowned heads on Burgstraat
new.desc: The house De Gekroonde Hoofden, from around 1560, carries a row of carved heads of the Counts of Flanders on its facade, beginning with Baldwin of Constantinople and ending with the Spanish king Philip II, with Charles V among them.
new.tip: Today it is a spare ribs restaurant. Look from the opposite pavement to take in the whole row, then walk on to the Prinsenhof where Charles V was born.

new.title: Have cake by the water at Julie's House
new.desc: A pastry house on the Kraanlei looking out over the Leie, near the Gravensteen. Pies, colourful cupcakes and breakfasts are made fresh every day in its own kitchen.
new.tip: Weekend breakfast fills up fast. Come mid-afternoon for a slice of pie and the view across to the Kraanlei facades.

new.title: Drink by candlelight at Café Rococo
new.desc: A small café in the Patershol lit only by candles, with an old-fashioned salon interior that feels like stepping back in time. It is one of the neighbourhood's favourite late-night hideaways.
new.tip: It opens late in the evening and fills up quickly at weekends, so arrive early. Best on a cold winter night.

new.title: Eat all the spare ribs you can at Amadeus
new.desc: In the narrow streets of the Patershol, Amadeus serves all-you-can-eat spare ribs with its well-known garlic sauce, in rooms with checked tablecloths and 1920s and 1930s decor.
new.tip: Book ahead, as tables fill up, especially at weekends. Pace yourself: the refills keep coming.

new.title: Eat Turkish pide on the Sleepstraat
new.desc: Just north of the Patershol, the Sleepstraat is known as the Turkish street of Ghent, lined with Turkish restaurants and shops. Pizza Gülhan is one of its big, busy, budget-friendly places for Turkish pizza and oven dishes.
new.tip: Share a pide or two with a glass of ayran, then browse the shops along the street for Turkish sweets.

new.title: Sweat it out at Aqua Azul in a 1911 merchant's house
new.desc: On the edge of the Patershol, this sauna and spa fills a former trading house from 1911 with an art nouveau interior. It is a warm city retreat a few steps from the Gravensteen.
new.tip: Book in advance. Tuesday afternoon is reserved for women.

new.title: Find the giant water lilies in the university's Botanical Garden
new.desc: On the edge of Citadelpark, Ghent University's botanical garden, founded at the end of the 18th century, grows about 10,000 plant species. In the Victoria greenhouse the huge leaves of Amazon water lilies float on the pond, and there are tropical, subtropical and succulent houses too.
new.tip: The garden and greenhouses are free and open daily. The university museum GUM, which next door tells science through doubt and failure, makes a good pair.

new.title: Sit among the vines at Sint-Pietersabdij
new.desc: Saint Amand founded this Benedictine abbey in the 7th century, and it grew rich on its estates and privileges. The cloisters, the quadrangle and the walled garden with its vineyard and ruin are free to wander; the upper floors host big exhibitions.
new.tip: On sunny days students study on the lawn, so bring a book. The ground floor and garden need no ticket.

new.title: Walk through the arena of the Wintercircus
new.desc: Built in 1885 as a circus, then a car workshop for decades, the Wintercircus reopened in 2024 after a prize-winning renovation. The old ring is now a covered public square, surrounded by a bakery, restaurants, an underground concert hall and a rooftop bar.
new.tip: Cut through it on your way from the Vooruit, and go up to the rooftop Bar Bassie for a view over the arts quarter.

new.title: Hear a concert in the old hospital at De Bijloke
new.desc: Ghent's music centre fills the buildings of the Bijloke hospital, founded over 700 years ago. The main hall, set in the former hospital ward, seats 960 and is home to the Symfonieorkest Vlaanderen, while the smaller Kraakhuis is made for chamber music.
new.tip: Programmes run from early music to jazz; check the calendar and book a seat in the main hall for the full effect of the old timber roof.

new.title: Lunch at De Appelier, Ghent's veggie pioneer
new.desc: Near Citadelpark in the arts quarter, De Appelier has served fully vegetarian daily specials for so long that the city calls it a pioneer of veggie food in Ghent.
new.tip: On weekday afternoons from 2 to 6 pm it turns into a coffee and cake stop, perfect after a museum visit.

new.title: Shop local at the Lousbergmarkt
new.desc: A covered market hall in the former cheese factory of Het Hinkelspel, where a bakery, an organic farm, the cheese makers and other local producers sell their goods side by side. A bar next door serves brunch and aperitifs.
new.tip: Put together a picnic of Hinkelspel cheese and CoPain bread and eat it along the water on the Lousbergskaai.

new.title: Join the students on the Overpoortstraat
new.desc: More than 35 student cafés stand shoulder to shoulder on this street just south of Sint-Pietersplein, with night shops, chip shops and pita bars in between. Ghent has over 66,000 students, and on a Thursday night it feels as if they are all here.
new.tip: Thursday is student night and can get wild. For a calmer look, come early in the evening and end with a cone of fries.

new.title: Light a candle at the Lourdes grotto of Oostakker
new.desc: In 1873 a marquise built a copy of the Lourdes grotto on her estate in Oostakker. After the reported healing of Pieter De Rudder in 1875 it became the most important Marian pilgrimage site in Flanders, and the neo-Gothic church built beside it was made a basilica in 1924.
new.tip: Come on a weekday for stillness, walk from the basilica to the grotto and its rows of candles, and watch how many locals still stop by.

new.title: Taste a fresh pour at Stroom brewery
new.desc: An independent brewery started by a Belgian and American duo, mixing traditional and progressive brewing and running on 100% renewable energy. The tasting room pours straight from the tap and fills growlers to take home.
new.tip: Guided tours with four tastings are for groups of eight or more, so bring friends, or just drop in for a glass.

new.title: Slurp ramen at Golden Gai near Dampoort
new.desc: A ramen bar near Gent-Dampoort station that makes its own noodles and sodas, using local ingredients where it can. Alongside four fixed ramens there is a monthly special, such as ramen with blood sausage.
new.tip: Three of the four ramens can be made vegetarian or vegan. Leave room for something from the cocktail list.

new.title: Have coffee among racing bikes at Bar Bidon
new.desc: On the Bisdomkaai near Portus Ganda, Bar Bidon is a coffee, breakfast and lunch bar for cycling fans, with fine bikes and gear on show between the tables.
new.tip: Take a seat on the terrace by the water; it makes a natural start or finish to a bike ride along the Schelde.

new.title: Hunt for a second-hand bike on the Oude Beestenmarkt
new.desc: On Sunday mornings the Oude Beestenmarkt near Portus Ganda hosts a market of second-hand bicycles, the Ghent way to find your next ride. By night the same square turns into a nightlife hub around Club 69.
new.tip: Check the date on the city's market calendar, bring cash and a lock, and always test-ride before you buy.

new.title: Explore the Arsenaal, an old railway yard gone creative
new.desc: Opened in 1881 as a workshop of the Belgian railways, the 12-hectare Arsenaal site in Gentbrugge is still full of sheds and tracks. Until it becomes a new neighbourhood, it hosts a bouldering gym, a skate academy, beach volleyball and makers of handmade bikes.
new.tip: Come on a Friday for the Moscou Market with fresh, artisanal produce, or check the site's calendar for design and maker fairs.

new.title: Walk the Gentbrugse Meersen
new.desc: On Ghent's east side, about 240 hectares of meadows, woods and ponds in a bend of the Schelde form part of the Scheldevallei National Park. Near the entrance it is all play and picnics; further north the area is left mostly to nature.
new.tip: Start at the Frans Tochpark by the Braemkasteel and follow the paths and boardwalks north; early morning is best for birds.

new.title: Dig for vintage treasures in a former church
new.desc: Wunderkammer Gent fills the former Saint Teresa of Avila church in Meulestede with second-hand and vintage furniture, lamps, art and curiosities, from design classics to affordable finds.
new.tip: The stock changes all the time, so check its social media for opening hours and come back often.

new.title: Find the Rubens in Aalst's unfinished Sint-Martinuskerk
new.desc: Work on Aalst's main church began around 1480 and dragged on for some 180 years, yet the money ran out before it reached its planned size or got its tower. Inside hang Rubens' 'Saint Roch appointed patron of plague victims' and a rare stone sacrament tower carved in 1604 by Jérôme Duquesnoy the Elder.
new.tip: A long restoration is under way, so parts may be closed; check before you go. The Grote Markt is a few steps away.

new.title: Find the golden spurs in Kortrijk's Onze-Lieve-Vrouwekerk
new.desc: After the Flemish militias beat the French knights outside Kortrijk on 11 July 1302, some 500 spurs taken from the dead were hung in this church. The originals were carried off in 1382, but replicas hang there today, and the Kortrijk 1302 exhibition now tells the story of the battle inside the church.
new.tip: Also look for Van Dyck's 'Raising of the Cross' behind the choir and the Counts' Chapel with its painted portraits of the counts of Flanders.

new.title: Learn why the Leie was called the golden river at Texture
new.desc: Until the 1960s the Leie region was the world's largest centre of flax production, and the river water used to process the fibre made it so profitable that the Leie became known as the golden river. Texture, in an old flax building on the river in Kortrijk, tells that story with fabrics you can touch.
new.tip: Have lunch at Kaffee Damast next door, then walk the Leie banks back towards the Broeltorens.

new.title: Step into Roger Raveel's white museum in Machelen
new.desc: In the Leie village of Machelen, where the painter lived and worked, architect Stéphane Beel built a white museum that opened in 1999. It holds over 300 paintings and hundreds of drawings by Roger Raveel, and his colourful 'poles of the unlimited' stand around the village.
new.tip: Cycle there along the Leie from Deinze, and walk around Machelen afterwards to spot the poles and the views Raveel painted.

new.title: Visit Count Egmont's castle in Zottegem
new.desc: Count Lamoraal van Egmont made this castle his home in 1566, two years before the Duke of Alva had him beheaded in Brussels. Restored between 2022 and 2024, it now houses the town library, and the park around it shows the outline of a 12th-century castle chapel.
new.tip: Library hours are your chance to see inside; the knights' hall is also used for concerts and weddings.

new.title: Follow the pink elephant to Brouwerij Huyghe in Melle
new.desc: Leon Huyghe founded this brewery in Melle in 1906 on a site where beer has reportedly been brewed since 1654. Its Delirium Tremens, first brewed in 1988 with three different yeasts, made the pink elephant famous across the world.
new.tip: Book the Delirium Experience with the brewery's beer museum online; Melle is a short train or bike ride from Ghent.

new.title: Drink a Gulden Draak at the brewery in Ertvelde
new.desc: Brouwerij Van Steenberge has brewed in Ertvelde in the Meetjesland since 1784, run by six generations of the same family. Its ruby-red Gulden Draak tripel shares its name with the golden dragon on top of Ghent's belfry.
new.tip: Bar Baptist above the brewery hosts tastings, some with a brewery tour first; plan your visit on the brewery's website.

new.title: Taste a Duchesse de Bourgogne at its brewery in Vichte
new.desc: The Verhaeghe family has brewed in Vichte, between Kortrijk and Oudenaarde, since the 1880s, and still matures its Flemish red-brown beers in big oak foeders. Its Duchesse de Bourgogne is a sweet and sour classic of the style.
new.tip: Guided tours with a tasting run daily by appointment for groups of seven or more. The brewery is about 100 m from Vichte station, but no trains stop there at weekends.

new.title: Have a beer by the Leie at 't Fonteintje in Kortrijk
new.desc: One of the oldest cafés in Kortrijk, this small protected building overlooks the Leie and is a locals' bar with a short but good beer list. Its name goes back to a street name from the late 1600s.
new.tip: In summer take a seat on the terrace by the river, and order the spaghetti if you are hungry.

new.title: Survive the cobbles of the Koppenberg
new.desc: Near Melden in the Flemish Ardennes, this 600-metre cobbled climb averages 11.6% and hits 22% in its steepest bend. It has featured in the Ronde van Vlaanderen dozens of times since 1976, and the road itself is a protected monument.
new.tip: Keep your weight back and stay seated so the rear wheel grips; if you stall, it is a long walk up. Avoid it when the stones are wet.

new.title: Wander the arboretum of Het Leen near Eeklo
new.desc: This provincial forest between Eeklo and Lievegem covers well over 250 hectares of mixed woods, heath and 15 ponds, with about 36 km of footpaths. Its arboretum holds more than 7,000 kinds of trees, shrubs and perennials.
new.tip: Drop into the forest museum, then finish at the cafeteria, which is closed on Mondays.

new.title: Walk the dike around the Molsbroek in Lokeren
new.desc: An 80-hectare marsh beside the Durme in Lokeren, ringed by a 4.5 km paved dike from which you watch wild waterbirds and marsh plants. The local nature group vzw Durme has looked after it since 1969.
new.tip: Start at the visitor centre on Molsbergenstraat on the eastern edge; bring binoculars.

new.title: Spot shovelers in the Bourgoyen-Ossemeersen
new.desc: On Ghent's western edge, 230 hectares of wet meadows flood every autumn and winter and draw so many northern shovelers that the area is an Important Bird Area. A 5.5 km loop passes two bird hides, the old Valkenhuis farm and a protected drainage windmill.
new.tip: Start at the nature centre on Driepikkelstraat, and come in winter with binoculars when the meadows are full of ducks.

new.title: Row on the Donkmeer, then eat eel the old way
new.desc: This 86-hectare lake in Berlare was dug out by peat cutters around 1800. Since the steam tram brought the first day-trippers in 1891 it has drawn people for boats, bikes and cafés, and the hamlet of Donk is known for its eel restaurants.
new.tip: Rent a boat or a bike to circle the lake, then order paling in 't groen, eel in a green herb sauce, at one of the lakeside restaurants.

new.title: Bird-watch in the Kalkense Meersen
new.desc: Between Kalken, Wetteren and Schellebelle lies the old floodplain of the Schelde, crossed by a river arm cut off when the Schelde was straightened. Now part of the Scheldevallei National Park, it is home to godwits, lapwings, marsh harriers, bluethroats and white storks.
new.tip: Cycle here from the Donkmeer nearby; spring is the best season for meadow birds.
